Afghan hound: One of the oldest known dog breeds, the Afghan hound was prized by ancient nobility for its ability to take down fast game like antelope in the rocky Afghan mountains — its long, silky coat evolved to protect it from brutal mountain cold.
African hunting dog: Not a domestic breed at all, but a wild African species also called the painted wolf — its scientific name Lycaon pictus literally means 'painted wolf,' and its patchy coat markings are as unique as a human fingerprint.
Airedale: Known as the 'King of Terriers' for being the largest of the terrier group, the Airedale was originally bred to hunt otters and rats along England's Aire River — a WWI Airedale named Jack even earned a posthumous medal for delivering a message under fire despite being wounded.
American Staffordshire terrier: Once known as 'Petey' from the classic Our Gang films, the American Staffordshire Terrier has a stocky, muscular build but moves with a surprisingly springy, confident gait.
Appenzeller: This tricolor Swiss herder from the Appenzell region nearly vanished in the early 1900s before dedicated breeders stepped in — today it remains the rarest of the four Swiss mountain dog breeds.
Australian Shepherd: Despite the name, the Australian Shepherd was actually developed by ranchers in the United States — its ancestors likely traveled from the Basque region of Spain by way of Australia before the breed took its modern form in California.
Australian terrier: Bred in Tasmania to hunt vermin in gold and opal mines, the Australian Terrier was the first new terrier breed the AKC had recognized in 21 years when it joined the club in 1960.
Bedlington terrier: With its arched back, pear-shaped head, and a fluffy lamb-style haircut, the Bedlington Terrier is often said to have 'the head of a lamb and the heart of a lion' — it was originally bred to hunt vermin and even badgers in a 19th-century English mining town.
Bernese mountain dog: Bred as an all-purpose Swiss farm dog for herding, guarding, and pulling carts, the Bernese Mountain Dog gets its name from the canton of Bern — its thick tri-color coat kept it warm while working in the Alps.
Bichon Frise: This cheerful little dog was such a favorite of French nobility that King Henry III reportedly carried his Bichons around in a basket slung from ribbons around his neck.
Black sable: Not a breed at all, but a coat-color pattern — sable dogs (seen famously in German Shepherds) have hairs with black tips over a lighter base, a look produced by the agouti gene that often darkens dramatically as a puppy grows into adulthood.
Blenheim spaniel: This chestnut-and-white coloring of the Cavalier King Charles Spaniel takes its name from Blenheim Palace, where the Dukes of Marlborough bred these dogs for generations — legend even credits a nervous duchess's thumbprint for the breed's signature spot on the forehead.
Border collie: Widely considered the smartest dog breed, the Border Collie can typically learn a new command in fewer than five repetitions, and one famous Border Collie named Chaser learned the names of over 1,000 individual objects.
Border terrier: Nicknamed for its distinctive 'otter head,' this scrappy little terrier was built with long enough legs to keep pace with a horse and a narrow enough body to squeeze underground after foxes.
Boston bull: Nicknamed the 'American Gentleman' for its tuxedo-like coat, the Boston Terrier was the first breed developed in the United States to earn AKC recognition, back in 1893.
Bouvier des Flandres: Its name literally translates to 'Cow Herder of Flanders' — this shaggy, powerful Belgian dog was originally an all-purpose farm worker that herded cattle, pulled carts, and even served as a messenger dog during World War I.
Brabancon griffo: Known in Europe as the Petit Brabançon (a smooth-coated cousin of the Brussels Griffon), this tiny bearded dog started out as a scrappy ratter for Brussels coachmen before a Belgian queen's fondness for the breed turned it into a fashionable lapdog.
Brittany spaniel: Despite its name, the Brittany isn't really a spaniel at all — it hunts by pointing and ranging far ahead like a setter, which is exactly why American breeders successfully petitioned to drop 'spaniel' from its official AKC name in 1982.
Cane Carso: Descended from Roman war dogs, the Cane Corso's name comes from the Latin 'cohors,' meaning guardian or protector — this muscular Italian breed nearly went extinct by the mid-20th century before a revival in the 1970s brought it back.
Cardigan: The Cardigan Welsh Corgi is the older of the two corgi breeds, arriving in Wales with the Celts around 1200 BC, and you can tell it apart from its Pembroke cousin by its long, fox-like tail.
Chesapeake Bay retriever: Descended from two Newfoundland-type puppies rescued from a shipwreck off Maryland in 1807, the Chesapeake Bay Retriever has an oily, water-resistant double coat and can retrieve upwards of 100-plus ducks from icy water in a single day.
Chihuahua: The world's smallest dog breed, the Chihuahua is also the only breed whose puppies are consistently born with a soft spot on the skull, called a 'molera,' much like a human infant's.
Chinese Crested Dog: This breed comes in two very different-looking varieties from the very same litter — the nearly bald Hairless and the fully coated Powderpuff — because hairlessness is a single dominant gene that not every puppy inherits.
Dandie Dinmont: This long-bodied terrier is the only AKC breed named after a fictional character — a farmer who resembled the dog-loving Dandie Dinmont from Sir Walter Scott's 1814 novel 'Guy Mannering' picked up the nickname, and it stuck to the breed too.
Doberman: Created in 1890s Germany by a tax collector named Louis Dobermann who wanted a loyal protector for his rounds, the Doberman Pinscher went on to make up an estimated 75 percent of U.S. military dogs during World War II.
English foxhound: Bred since the 1600s by crossing scent-tracking stag hounds with speedy Greyhound types, the English Foxhound has such high stamina it can run for hours — most today still live and work in hunt-club packs rather than as house pets.
English setter: Nearly every English Setter today traces back to the breeding work of Englishman Edward Laverack, who started his line in 1825 and later literally wrote the book on the breed.
English springer: Springer Spaniels and Cocker Spaniels actually used to be the very same breed — puppies from the same litter were simply sorted by size, with the bigger ones becoming Springers, until the two were split into separate breeds around 1900.
EntleBucher: The smallest of Switzerland's four Sennenhund mountain dog breeds, the Entlebucher is nicknamed the 'Laughing Dog of the Alps' for its perpetually cheerful expression while herding cattle.
Eskimo dog: Despite its name, the American Eskimo Dog was never actually a sled dog — this fluffy, all-white breed descends from German Spitz dogs and became famous in the early 1900s as a tightrope-walking circus performer with Barnum & Bailey.
Fila Braziliero: Bred in Brazil from Mastiff, Bloodhound, and Bulldog ancestors, the Fila Brasileiro is famous for its 'never forget, never forsake' loyalty to its family — its name comes from the Portuguese word 'filar,' meaning to hold fast, describing its job of pinning large game without seriously injuring it.
French bulldog: The French Bulldog's signature upright 'bat ears' actually caused a transatlantic dog-show dispute — when an English judge favored the alternative rounded 'rose ear' at Westminster in 1897, outraged American fans founded their own breed club to protect the bat-ear standard.
German shepherd: Made globally famous by the 1920s movie star dog Rin Tin Tin, who was rescued from a World War I battlefield in France and went on to headline 23 Hollywood films.
German short haired pointer: A true all-purpose gundog, the German Shorthaired Pointer can point, retrieve, and track on land or in water thanks to its webbed feet, and it remains the most popular pointing breed in the AKC's Sporting Group.
Gordon setter: The only setter breed developed in Scotland, the Gordon Setter was refined by the fourth Duke of Gordon in the early 1800s and is the largest of all the setter breeds.
Great Dane: Nicknamed the 'Apollo of Dogs' for its majestic size, the Great Dane actually originated in Germany, not Denmark, and the tallest dog ever recorded — a Great Dane named Zeus — measured over seven feet tall standing on his hind legs.
Great Pyrenees: Bred for thousands of years to guard flocks alone on snowy mountaintops, the Great Pyrenees was trusted to think independently and make its own decisions about threats without a shepherd's direction.
Greater Swiss Mountain dog: The largest and oldest of Switzerland's four Sennenhund breeds, the Greater Swiss Mountain Dog was once nicknamed the 'poor man's horse' for its job hauling carts loaded with dairy goods through the Alps.
Ibizan hound: This elegant sighthound's history stretches back some 5,000 years to ancient Egypt — a life-size statue of the jackal-god Anubis found in Tutankhamen's tomb looks remarkably like the Ibizan Hound of today, and the breed can leap an impressive six feet straight up from a standstill.
Irish setter: Known for its flashy mahogany-red coat and 'rollicking' personality per the official AKC standard, the Irish Setter matures slowly and tends to keep a puppy-like spirit well into adulthood.
Irish terrier: Nicknamed the 'daredevil of terriers' for its fearless, fiery personality, the Irish Terrier served as a trench messenger dog on the Western Front during World War I, carrying communications under fire.
Irish water spaniel: Sometimes called the 'clown of the spaniel family,' this tall, curly-coated swimmer has a distinctive smooth, tapering 'rat tail' that acts like a rudder while paddling.
Irish wolfhound: The tallest of all dog breeds, the Irish Wolfhound can stand over seven feet tall on its hind legs, yet despite its size and history as a big-game hunter, it's famous for being a gentle giant with a sweet, friendly temperament.
Italian greyhound: A favorite lapdog of Mediterranean and later Renaissance nobility for over 2,000 years, the Italian Greyhound is a genuine miniature hunter that can still reach speeds up to 25 miles per hour despite its dainty, toy-sized build.
Japanese Spitzes: This perpetually smiling, all-white companion breed was developed in Japan in the 1920s-40s from spitz-type dogs imported from countries like Canada, the US, and China — and unlike many breeds, it was bred purely to be a companion from the very start.
Japanese spaniel: Known today as the Japanese Chin, this cat-like little dog was once so prized by Japanese and Chinese royalty that commoners were forbidden from owning one — some were even bred to be small enough to be carried in a kimono sleeve.
Kerry blue terrier: Ireland's national terrier, the Kerry Blue is born jet black and gradually 'clears' to its namesake blue-gray coat as it matures — it was even reportedly nominated by Irish nationalist Michael Collins to become Ireland's official national dog.
Labrador retriever: America's most popular dog breed for over 25 years running, the Labrador Retriever actually descends from a now-extinct working breed called the St. John's Water Dog and has webbed toes built for swimming.
Lakeland terrier: Named for England's scenic Lake District, this small but bold farm dog was bred to work in packs chasing off sheep-stealing foxes, and its wiry, low-shedding coat makes it a popular pick for allergy sufferers.
Leonberg: Created in the mid-1800s by a German town politician who wanted a dog resembling the lion on Leonberg's town crest, the Leonberger's males grow a dramatic lion-like mane around the neck and chest.
Lhasa: Bred by Buddhist monks in Tibet to guard monasteries from the inside — while larger mastiffs guarded outside — the Lhasa Apso's original Tibetan name, Abso Seng Kye, translates to 'Bark Lion Sentinel Dog.'
Maltese dog: One of the oldest toy breeds in existence, the Maltese was such a beloved status symbol among Roman noblewomen over 2,000 years ago that it earned the nickname 'The Comforter' for its soothing companionship.
Mexican hairless: Known as the Xoloitzcuintli, this roughly 3,000-year-old breed is named after the Aztec god Xolotl and was believed to guide souls safely to the afterlife — it comes in both hairless and coated varieties and was a favorite of artists Frida Kahlo and Diego Rivera.
Newfoundland: A gentle giant with webbed feet and a water-resistant triple coat, the Newfoundland is such a powerful swimmer that it can tow small boats and has been trained as a genuine canine lifeguard.
Norfolk terrier: Originally considered the same breed as the Norwich Terrier, the drop-eared version was split off and named the Norfolk in 1964 — a handy memory trick is that the 'folk' in Norfolk sounds like 'fold,' just like its folded-over ears.
Norwegian elkhound: A true Viking-era companion, the Norwegian Elkhound was bred to track and corner moose — called 'elg' in Norway — and can reportedly catch a scent from over a mile away, with Vikings even burying their Elkhounds alongside their families.
Norwich terrier: The prick-eared cousin of the Norfolk Terrier, the Norwich was originally bred to rid Cambridge University dormitories of rats, and remains one of the smallest working terriers in the AKC lineup.
Old English sheepdog: Nicknamed the 'Bobtail,' this shaggy drover dog traditionally had its tail docked to prove it was a working farm dog exempt from an old English dog tax — and every spring farmers used to shear its thick coat right alongside the sheep's.
Pekinese: So sacred in China that only imperial royalty was legally allowed to own one, the Pekingese was bred to resemble a miniature lion and was sometimes carried hidden in a noble's sleeve as a pint-sized guard dog.
Pembroke: Queen Elizabeth II owned more than 30 Pembroke Welsh Corgis over her lifetime, starting with a dog named Susan given to her as an 18th-birthday present — and unlike its popular stub-tailed image, the breed is naturally born with a long tail.
Pomeranian: Pomeranians used to weigh up to 30 pounds until Queen Victoria fell for a small 12-pound specimen in 1888 and began favoring smaller dogs in her breeding program, roughly halving the breed's average size within her lifetime.
Rhodesian ridgeback: Nicknamed the 'African Lion Hound,' the Rhodesian Ridgeback was bred in southern Africa to track and hold lions at bay for hunters — never to kill them — and is instantly recognizable by the distinctive ridge of backward-growing hair along its spine.
Rottweiler: Descended from Roman cattle-droving mastiffs that marched with the legions over 2,000 years ago, the Rottweiler gets its name from the German town of Rottweil, where it later worked as a butcher's dog, even carrying the day's earnings in a pouch around its neck.
Saint Bernard: These legendary Alpine rescue dogs were bred by monks at a Swiss hospice, and the most famous of them all, a dog named Barry, is credited with saving more than 40 lives in the early 1800s — his preserved body is still on display in a Swiss museum today.
Saluki: Known as the 'Royal Dog of Egypt,' the Saluki is one of the oldest domesticated dog breeds, with images of slender, feather-eared hounds appearing on Egyptian tomb art more than 5,000 years ago — some were even mummified alongside pharaohs.
Samoyed: Samoyeds have an upturned mouth known as the 'Samoyed smile' — it's not just adorable, it actually stops the dog from drooling icicles in freezing Siberian temperatures.
Scotch terrier: Known today as the Scottish Terrier, this feisty little breed became a White House icon thanks to Fala, President Franklin D. Roosevelt's beloved companion and one of the most famous presidential pets in history.
Scottish deerhound: Once called the 'Royal Dog of Scotland,' this towering sighthound was so prized that for centuries no one below the rank of earl was allowed to own one.
Sealyham terrier: This rare Welsh terrier had a real Hollywood streak — Alfred Hitchcock loved his two Sealyhams so much he gave them a cameo appearance in his film The Birds.
Shetland sheepdog: Shelties are ranked the 6th most intelligent dog breed in the world, and early members of the breed standing just 8-10 inches tall were once nicknamed 'toonie dogs' after the Shetland word for farm.
Shiba Dog: The Shiba Inu is the smallest of Japan's six native spitz breeds and one of the most ancient, originally bred to flush small game out of dense mountain brushwood that its reddish coat helped it blend into.
Shih Tzu: The name Shih Tzu means 'lion dog' in Mandarin, honoring a breed developed in Tibetan monasteries to resemble the lions sacred in Buddhist legend, and later so treasured by Chinese royalty it was never sold to outsiders.
Siberian husky: Huskies often have one blue eye and one brown due to heterochromia, and their sled-pulling heritage became legend in 1925 when teams of them raced serum across Alaska to stop a diphtheria outbreak in Nome.
Staffordshire bullterrier: Despite their muscular build, Staffordshire Bull Terriers earned the affectionate nickname 'the Nanny Dog' for their long history of gentleness and patience with children.
Sussex spaniel: Unlike most spaniels, the low-slung Sussex was bred to bark and howl while trailing game through thick cover, letting hunters who couldn't see it through the brush follow its voice instead.
Tibetan mastiff: This massive guardian breed's history stretches back thousands of years on the Tibetan plateau, and Tibetan legend holds that Tibetan Mastiffs carry the souls of monks and nuns who weren't yet ready to reach paradise.
Tibetan terrier: Despite the name, this isn't a true terrier at all — it's an ancient companion breed from Tibetan monasteries once considered such good luck charms that they were never sold, only given as gifts.
Walker hound: Also known as the Treeing Walker Coonhound, this fast, sharp-nosed hunter traces back to a legendary 1800s dog named Tennessee Lead, whose speed transformed the breed's hunting ability forever.
Weimaraner: Nicknamed the 'Gray Ghost' for its sleek coat and stealthy hunting style, this breed was once so exclusive to German nobility that dogs sold outside their private club were secretly neutered first.
Welsh springer spaniel: One of Britain's oldest sporting breeds, red-and-white spaniels resembling today's Welsh Springer appear in Welsh art and law dating as far back as the 6th century.
West Highland white terrier: Legend says the Westie's snow-white coat exists because a Scottish colonel, after mistakenly shooting his own wheaten-colored terrier during a hunt, began breeding only white dogs so he'd never make that mistake again.
Yorkshire terrier: Long before becoming a glamorous lapdog, the Yorkie was a scrappy working-class ratter that kept vermin out of English textile mills and coal mines.
affenpinscher: The Affenpinscher's name literally means 'monkey terrier' in German, a nod to its wiry eyebrows, beard, and mischievous, monkey-like expression.
basenji: The basenji can't bark because of its uniquely shaped larynx — instead, when it gets excited it lets out a yodel-like sound nicknamed the 'baroo.'
basset: That long, low body and those droopy ears aren't just for looks — the ears actually help sweep scent particles up off the ground toward the Basset Hound's nose.
beagle: Beagles pack around 220 million scent receptors into their noses, compared to a human's roughly 5 million, making their sense of smell thousands of times more powerful than ours.
black and tan coonhound: This deep-voiced hunter has such a distinctive baying howl that owners can often recognize their own dog's voice from a great distance across the woods.
bloodhound: A Bloodhound's nose holds about 230 million scent receptors, and it's famous for being the first animal whose scent-tracking evidence was ever accepted in a court of law.
bluetick: The Bluetick Coonhound is Tennessee's official state dog, and it inspired 'Old Blue,' the beloved hunting dog immortalized in Fred Gipson's classic novel Old Yeller.
borzoi: Once known as the Russian Wolfhound, the elegant Borzoi could only be given as a gift from the Tsar — Russian nobility never allowed them to be bought or sold.
boxer: Boxers get their playful name from their habit of standing on their hind legs and 'boxing' with their front paws when excited or at play.
briard: Thomas Jefferson, famously no fan of dogs, fell for the Briard so completely that he brought a pregnant one home from France aboard his ship in 1789, and she had puppies during the Atlantic crossing.
bull mastiff: Nicknamed the 'Gamekeeper's Night Dog,' this powerful breed was created in 19th-century England to silently track and pin down poachers on hunting estates without making a sound.
cairn: The most famous Cairn Terrier in history is Terry, the female rescue dog who played Toto in The Wizard of Oz — and earned a weekly salary higher than most of her human co-stars.
chinese rural dog: Rather than a single breed, this refers to the indigenous village dogs found across rural China, a group with some of the most genetically diverse and ancient domestic dog ancestry on Earth, tracing back over 15,000 years.
chow: Chow Chows are one of only two dog breeds born with a blue-black tongue, and no one is entirely sure why — though Chinese folklore blames a dog that once licked ink spilled from the night sky.
clumber: The heaviest and most sedate of all spaniels, the Clumber was a favorite of British royalty like Prince Albert and King Edward VII, who nicknamed it the 'sporting tank' of the spaniel world.
cocker spaniel: The Cocker Spaniel was the single most popular dog breed in America throughout the entire decade of the 1950s, boosted by pop-culture stars like Disney's Lady from Lady and the Tramp.
collie: Queen Victoria fell in love with Collies during an 1860s visit to the Scottish Highlands and brought them into her royal kennels, kicking off a wave of popularity the breed still enjoys thanks to Lassie decades later.
curly coated retriever: One of the oldest retriever breeds in existence, the Curly-Coated Retriever was already a recognized show class in England more than 40 years before Golden and Labrador Retrievers got their own breed status.
dhole: The dhole, or Asiatic wild dog, is a wild species native to South and Southeast Asia that doesn't bark or howl at all — instead it communicates across the forest with an eerie, high-pitched whistle.
dingo: The dingo is a wild canid that arrived in Australia thousands of years ago and is the continent's largest surviving land predator, with a taxonomic classification still debated by scientists today.
flat coated retriever: Nicknamed the 'Peter Pan' of the dog world, the Flat-Coated Retriever matures slowly and keeps its goofy, puppy-like exuberance well into adulthood.
giant schnauzer: Bred in Bavaria to drive cattle to market, Giant Schnauzers later found work guarding beer wagons and breweries — a job that suited their naturally protective instincts perfectly.
golden retriever: The Golden Retriever's origin story begins on a single Scottish estate, Guisachan, where a 19th-century Scottish lord spent decades carefully breeding the friendly, golden-coated dog we know today.
groenendael: Named after breeder Nicolas Rose's château, Chateau Groenendael, this all-black Belgian Sheepdog variety was originally almost named the 'Rose' after him before he chose the estate's name instead.
keeshond: Once the mascot of Dutch canal barges, the fluffy Keeshond became a political symbol during 18th-century unrest in the Netherlands and remains a beloved emblem of Dutch national pride today.
kelpie: Australian Kelpies are famous for their agile herding style — when a flock is too tightly packed to move around, a Kelpie will simply run across the backs of the sheep to get where it needs to go.
komondor: The Komondor's shaggy white coat naturally forms itself into thick cords that look like dreadlocks, both camouflaging it among the sheep it guards and acting like armor against predator attacks.
kuvasz: This Hungarian guardian breed was so trusted by 15th-century King Matthias Corvinus that he reportedly kept it closer to him than his own royal guardsmen.
malamute: One of the oldest Arctic sled breeds, the Alaskan Malamute isn't built for speed but for power — it's the heavyweight freighter of the sled dog world, bred to haul heavy loads over long distances.
malinois: Belgian Malinois are favored by elite military units partly because they're excellent skydivers — their lighter build compared to German Shepherds makes tandem parachute jumps easier for their handlers.
miniature pinscher: Nicknamed the 'King of Toys' for its proud, high-stepping gait, the Miniature Pinscher is often mistaken for a shrunken Doberman, even though the Min Pin's history actually predates the Doberman Pinscher.
miniature poodle: Bred down in size from the Standard Poodle partly so they'd be easier to transport, Miniature Poodles became star performers in traveling European circuses thanks to their sharp intelligence and trainability.
miniature schnauzer: Unlike most AKC terriers, the Miniature Schnauzer has no British ancestry at all — it was bred entirely in Germany from its larger Standard Schnauzer cousin to be an expert barnyard ratter.
otterhound: Rarer than the giant panda, with fewer than 1,000 left worldwide, the shaggy Otterhound has webbed feet built for swimming and even played Sandy the dog in the 1982 movie musical Annie.
papillon: The Papillon gets its name from the French word for 'butterfly,' inspired by its large, fringed ears that fan out just like a butterfly's wings.
pug: Chinese emperors once assigned personal guards to protect their Pugs, prizing them so much that their forehead wrinkles were said to resemble the Chinese character for 'prince.'
redbone: Redbone Coonhounds became famous far beyond the hunting world after starring as Old Dan and Little Ann in the beloved novel and film Where the Red Fern Grows.
schipperke: Belgian barge captains nicknamed this small black dog the 'Little Captain' for its habit of patrolling canal boats as a ratter and watchdog.
silky terrier: Developed in Australia in the 1890s by crossing Yorkshire Terriers with Australian Terriers, the Silky Terrier was bred purely as a companion — but it's still tough enough to have a reputation for killing snakes.
soft coated wheaten terrier: For centuries, Irish law reserved hounds and other 'gentry' breeds for the upper classes, so ordinary farmers relied on the versatile Wheaten Terrier to herd, hunt, and guard their land instead.
standard poodle: Despite being France's national dog, the Poodle actually originated in Germany, where its name comes from 'pudel,' meaning 'to splash in water' — a nod to its original job as a duck retriever.
standard schnauzer: The Standard Schnauzer is the original of the three schnauzer breeds, with a history as a German farm ratter and guard dog stretching back to at least the 15th century.
teddy: 'Teddy' isn't a distinct dog breed at all — it's a popular grooming style, usually given to small poodles or poodle mixes, that trims the coat into a round, plush, teddy-bear-like shape.
toy poodle: Toy Poodles were beloved by French royalty, including King Louis XVI, and later became star circus performers thanks to their sharp intelligence and love of an audience.
toy terrier: The tiny English Toy Terrier was originally bred for the brutal Victorian-era 'sport' of rat-baiting, and one especially fast specimen reportedly killed 300 rats in under an hour back in 1848.
vizsla: Vizslas are famously affectionate, earning them the nickname 'Velcro dog' for how closely they like to stick to their owner's side at all times.
whippet: Nicknamed the 'poor man's racehorse,' the Whippet is believed to have the fastest idle-to-full-speed acceleration of any dog breed, capable of reaching 35 miles per hour in seconds.
wire haired fox terrier: The Wire Fox Terrier has won Best in Show at the Westminster Kennel Club Dog Show more times than any other breed in the show's history.
